title: The Store Clerk Who Kept Winning the Lottery #shorts

lines.text: An old man's lottery ticket won a quarter of a million dollars, and the store clerk told him it won a free ticket.
He'd played the lottery for years. When the clerk checked his ticket, the machine jingled twice.
She smiled, handed him a free ticket, and kept the real one.
A few days later, he opened the local paper. The big winner? The clerk from his store.
So he complained to the lottery company. They fought him instead.
He had to take them to court, and it dragged on for years.
Then, on the day the trial was supposed to start, they suddenly settled, and made him promise not to talk about it.
But a TV news team got curious. If one clerk did this, how many others had?
They asked a math professor to check the numbers.
Store workers had won over two hundred big prizes. By luck alone, it should have been about sixty.
You see, clerks don't buy way more tickets than everybody else, so they shouldn't win way more either.
It's like a friend who wins every coin toss, but he's also the one who flips the coin and tells you how it landed.
The odds of that being luck were about one in a trillion trillion trillion trillion.
Now you can scan your own ticket, and the screen faces you.
And the lottery company? It spent three times more on lawyers fighting the old man than it ever paid him.

sources: Ontario Ombudsman, 'A Game of Trust' backgrounder (2007): July 2001, Bob Edmonds checks his tickets in the Coboconk variety store, hears the machine jingle twice but receives only a free ticket; the clerk and her husband claim the prize; Edmonds reads about the win in the local paper; OLG settles with Edmonds for $200,000

Ontario Ombudsman, 'A Game of Trust' fact sheet: Bob Edmonds case: $200,000 in settlement; $629,600 in legal costs; Seven-Point Plan with $10 million for ticket checkers; 247 major insider wins since 1999
Tampa Bay Times / AP (2007): the OLG settled with Edmonds the day his trial was to begin in 2005, paying him $200,000
Wikipedia, 'Bob Edmonds': the $250,000 ticket; 2005 out-of-court settlement with a non-disclosure agreement; the fifth estate expose of October 2006

Globe and Mail via probability.ca, 'Lottery insiders win big bucks': more than 200 insiders won prizes of $50,000 or more since 1999; fewer than 60 should have by chance (statistician Jeffrey Rosenthal); odds of one in a trillion trillion trillion trillion (Wikipedia, OLG)
CBC the fifth estate update (2006): OLG plans electronic devices at every location so players can check their own tickets, larger win text on screens, and signed tickets
